description_full: The Sherwin-Williams Company engages in the development, manufacture, distribution, and sale of paint, coatings, and related products to professional, industrial, commercial and retail customers. The company operates through three segments: Paint Stores Group, Consumer Brands Group, and Performance Coatings Group. The Paint Stores Group segment offers architectural paint and coatings; protective and marine products; and OEM product finishes and related products for architectural and industrial paint contractors, and do-it-yourself homeowners under the Sherwin-Williams brand. The Consumer Brands Group segment supplies a portfolio of branded and private-label architectural paints, stains, varnishes, industrial products, wood finishes products, wood preservatives, applicators, corrosion inhibitors, aerosols, caulks, and adhesives to retailers, including home centers and hardware stores, and dedicated dealers and distributors. The Performance Coatings Group segment develops and sells industrial coatings for wood finishing and general industrial applications; automotive refinish products; protective and marine coatings; coil coatings; packaging coatings; and performance-based resins and colorants. This segment serves retailers, dealers, jobbers, licensees, and other third-party distributors. The company operates in North America, South America, the Caribbean, Europe, Asia, and Australia. The Sherwin-Williams Company was founded in 1866 and is headquartered in Cleveland, Ohio.

financial_summary: Sherwin-Williams Company (The) is a large-cap basic materials business with a $84.5B market cap on $23.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +8% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 22% against a 9% cost of capital — a 13-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 45%.

The business throws off $2.7B in free cash flow — roughly 11 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.34× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.6× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 8.2×.
Shareholder yield is only 0.9%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 6.3% of the shares.

Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $163 (margin of safety -115%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 35%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $127 to $210 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.

prof: ROIC of 22% clears the cost of capital of 8.6% by 13pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.41).
It runs a 45% gross margin and converts 11% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.34x.
ROE of 56% is amplified by 5.6x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.

hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.6x net debt to EBITDA ($207.2M of cash against $10.9B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 8.2x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.8, in the safe zone).
The current ratio of 0.87 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 2.1% over 3 years, 5.1% over 5 years and 7.6% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 33% of profits supports about 7.1% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -3.1% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs 2.3x depreciation (3.4% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 16, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 6.3%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 85%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (7 sales, net $10.8M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.9% (0.9% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.5% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 40 consecutive years, raising it 10.1% a year over the last five.
